article.overview: A robotic sample scoop is a mechanical surface sampler that collects loose lunar regolith and small fragments by digging, scraping or sweeping material into a collection chamber or container. It is usually mounted on a robotic arm or a lander mechanism and operated by commands from Earth. Scoops are suited to loose surface material because they can acquire a sample quickly with relatively simple hardware. This article covers the scoop-type sampler class and three documented examples: the Surveyor III Soil Mechanics Surface Sampler [1][2], the Chang'e-5 surface sampling system [4][5][6], and the crewed Apollo 11 contingency sample collector, included only for comparison [3].
article.description: A robotic sample scoop is a mechanical surface sampler that collects loose material by digging, scraping or sweeping it into a collection chamber. In a lunar mission, the scoop is typically driven by a motorised arm or lander mechanism. Scoops are most useful where the target is loose surface material. They are less suited to intact rock cores or material from depth, which usually requires a drill, and the material they collect is disturbed and may be mixed, so the position and depth of collection must be recorded carefully. Two flown examples illustrate the design space. Surveyor III carried a soil mechanics surface sampler that could dig trenches and test the soil's mechanical properties [1][2]. Chang'e-5 used a scoop on a robotic arm within its surface sampling sequence, followed by sealing the samples into a return container [5][6].
article.scientific_purpose_and_applications: The purpose of a sample scoop is to bring extraterrestrial material to a place where it can be analysed, either by instruments on the spacecraft or in laboratories on Earth. For the Moon, this material can reveal regolith composition, grain size, density and mechanical behaviour, and in sample return missions it provides material for laboratory study. Chang'e-5 soils collected from scooped sample bottles were characterised in the laboratory, with reported values for particle size, bulk density, true density and specific surface area [4]. Surveyor III's sampler was used to test soil strength in situ, with bearing tests and trenching reported [1][2]. The same type of tool can therefore serve both engineering characterisation and sample collection, although these purposes need different design choices.
article.operating_principle: A scoop works by penetrating the surface with a leading edge, collecting material into a bucket or sampler head, and then retracting or rotating so that the material is retained. The Surveyor III soil mechanics surface sampler was modified from its planned configuration. The design removed the strain, acceleration and position sensing systems and added a means of measuring motor current during operation, which suited the spacecraft's reduced telemetry and command capability [1]. For Chang'e-5, the published sources describe two samplers. Sampler A collects loose regolith and deposits it into the container. Sampler B collects sticky material by coring into the ground with toothed metal flaps [5]. Secondary reporting describes a scoop on the robotic arm end effector [6], but no source consulted explicitly maps the scoop onto Sampler A. Collected material is transferred into a container that must be sealed to protect the sample during return [5][6].
article.scientific_importance: Scoop-type samplers are one of the most direct ways to obtain lunar surface material, and sample return missions depend on reliable acquisition and containment. The Surveyor III sampler showed that a robotic scoop could disturb and characterise lunar soil in place [1][2]. The Chang'e-5 mission combined a scoop on a robotic arm with a drill and a sealed return container. A deputy chief designer at the China Academy of Space Technology described the whole process of taking and sealing samples as one the team had never previously carried out [6]. Scientific value depends on a documented location, depth, method and handling chain for each sample, because these determine how the returned material can be interpreted.

physical_specifications.note: There is no universal mass, size or power figure for a robotic sample scoop. Designs vary with the arm or mechanism, the target material, the sample container and the mission duration. The examples below describe specific instruments. Their figures apply only to those instruments and should not be generalised. Dimensions, masses and power are given only where a source states them.

physical_specifications.dimensions_and_proportions: No single dimension applies to robotic sample scoops. Surveyor III's sampler reach (1.5 m) and digging depth (18 cm) are reported [2], but its overall dimensions are not stated in the sources consulted. Chang'e-5's two samplers are reported at about 35 cm and about 30 cm long [5]. The Apollo 11 collector's dimensions are not specified [3]. A new scoop's dimensions would depend on its arm, target material and container.
physical_specifications.mass_and_weight: Surveyor III sampler mass not publicly specified in verified sources. The 997.9 kg figure belongs to the whole spacecraft [2]. Chang'e-5 surface sampling and packing system reported at 1.5 kg, including a 360 g sample container [5]. This is a whole-system figure, not a scoop-only figure. Apollo 11 collector mass not specified [3].
physical_specifications.power_requirements: Not publicly specified in verified sources for the Surveyor III sampler, the Chang'e-5 system or the Apollo 11 collector. Surveyor III's sampler was modified to measure motor current during operation [1], but no power value was found.

article.environmental_and_operational_requiremen: A surface scoop must operate in vacuum, under extreme temperature swings, in abrasive dust. The Chang'e-5 system's 200 °C design target and 130 °C camera limit show that thermal protection is a design constraint [5]. The Surveyor III hardware was exposed to the lunar surface for about two and a half years before retrieval [2]. Remote operation is constrained by command and telemetry capacity. The Surveyor III sampler was modified because of reduced telemetry and command capability [1]. Sample handling also needs contamination control. The Chang'e-5 team described a high vacuum sealing device designed to keep samples intact [6].
article.limitations: A scoop samples shallow, loose or disturbed material. It is not designed to recover intact cores and cannot in general establish stratigraphy, depth or the in-situ state of rock. Material collected by scoop can be mixed during collection, so the location and depth of each sample must be recorded. A scoop that is designed for loose regolith may also be less effective in dense or sticky material, as the Chang'e-5 design's separate sticky-material sampler suggests [5].

transportation_and_deployment.overview: A robotic sample scoop can be delivered to the Moon as part of a lander or sample return mission. For a surface payload, the sequence includes Earth integration, launch, lunar transfer, landing, deployment on the surface, arm or mechanism setup, power and data connection, and thermal and mechanical interface checks. For a sample return payload, the critical constraints are containment, sealing, transfer and the return chain.
transportation_process: Integrate the scoop or sampling mechanism into the lander or spacecraft payload on Earth.
Launch and transfer to the Moon.
Land and deploy the arm or sampling mechanism on the surface.
Collect the sample into a container and seal it.
Transfer the sealed container to the ascent or return vehicle, as in the Chang'e-5 sequence [6].
transportation_and_deployment.deployment_methods: Surveyor III's sampler was commanded from Earth on the surface [1][2]. Chang'e-5 used a robotic arm for surface collection, following a drilling phase [6]. Setup, thermal protection and interface checks depend on the specific lander and arm.
transportation_and_deployment.historical_examples: Surveyor III (1967 operations; hardware retrieved in 1969) and Chang'e-5 (2020) are flown examples of robotic surface sampling. The Apollo 11 contingency collector is a crewed comparison [3].
transportation_and_deployment.compatibility_assessment: No compatibility with a named lander, rover or spacecraft is asserted, because no verified interface evidence was found for this payload.

article.historical_significance: The Surveyor III sampler was an early robotic test of lunar soil mechanics, and its retrieved hardware was studied after long exposure on the Moon [1][2]. The Apollo 11 contingency collector is a historical example of early sample collection, although it was crewed [3]. The Chang'e-5 surface sampling system is a more recent flown example of a robotic scoop used within a complete sample return chain [5][6].
article.limitations_and_uncertainties: Most numerical values for the Chang'e-5 system come from a university press article and a news report rather than CNSA technical documentation [5][6]. The Surveyor III sampler's mass, dimensions and power are not stated in the sources consulted. The full text of its NASA preliminary report was not available for review [1]. Published counts of its trenching and soil tests differ between summaries [2]. The Chang'e-5 sample quantity is disputed between sources [5][6]. Luna-series sample-return reports were not used as scoop examples because the sources consulted differ on whether those missions used a scoop or a drill, and this was not resolved against a primary technical source. No direct image asset URL was verified for any image in this article. The NASA Apollo Lunar Surface Journal tools index returned a 404 error during research, and a Chang'e-5 aerospace article returned a 403 error.

image_handling.url_policy: All URL values in this file have query strings and fragments removed. No direct image asset URL was verified, so every image_url is null and only linked source-page references are used.

data_quality_notes: Research used 8 WebSearch calls and about 9 page reads. No MCP tools were used. The NASA Apollo Lunar Surface Journal tools index returned 404, and the Chang'e-5 aerospace article (MDPI) returned 403. The eoPortal Chang'e-5 page contained no mission content.

Surveyor III sampler: mass, dimensions and power not verified. The NTRS record for NASA SP-146 showed no downloadable full text. Trench and test counts differ between the NASA summary (4 trenches, 4 bearing tests, 13 impact tests) and a separate preliminary summary seen in search results (8 bearing tests, 14 impact tests).

Chang'e-5 scoop: the arm and scoop description comes from secondary reporting (Spaceflight Now [6]) and from search results, not a primary CNSA paper. No source consulted maps the scoop explicitly onto Sampler A [5].
Chang'e-5 sample quantity: PolyU reports 2 kg acquired [5]; Spaceflight Now reports no official estimate and a goal of more than 2 kg [6]. Treated as disputed.
Apollo 11 contingency collector: crewed and hand-operated, included only as a comparison. Total 1015.29 g, fines 492.12 g and rocks 522 g (text) do not exactly reconcile [3].
Luna-series sample-return missions were excluded as scoop examples because sources consulted differ on whether they used a scoop or a drill.
Image: one linked source-page reference only (Surveyor 3 Apollo 12 EVA photograph). No direct asset URL was verified, so image_url is null for all images.
